title: How to Set Realistic Retirement Goals With Variable Income
description: Planning for the future when you don't know what you'll earn next month.
content:
Standard retirement calculators assume a steady paycheck that grows by 3% a year. For the 60 million Americans with variable income—Realtors, Consultants, Gig Workers, and Business Owners—this model is broken. You cannot simply 'automate $500 a month' if your income swings from $10,000 to $0. Planning for retirement on variable income requires a dynamic strategy that captures the upside of 'Feast' months while protecting you during 'Famine' months. This guide adapts traditional retirement math for the irregular earner.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Percentage' Rule: Instead of a fixed dollar amount, commit to saving a fixed percentage (e.g., 20%) of every deposit. This automatically scales your savings up when income is high.
  • The 'Baseline' Budget: Build your retirement plan based on your lowest reliable income year, not your average. Treat windfall years as bonus acceleration, not the norm.
  • The Solo 401(k): Use this vehicle to make massive 'Employer' profit-sharing contributions (up to ~$69k) during good years to make up for years where you can't save max amounts.
  • Cash Buffer Multiplier: Variable earners need a larger liquid emergency fund (9-12 months) in retirement to avoid selling stocks during a market dip combined with a slow income year.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Self-employed individuals pay the full 15.3% SE Tax, meaning your 'Net' income for saving is lower than a W-2 peer. However, the ability to deduct business expenses and use the Solo 401(k) offers higher potential tax savings if managed correctly.

The 'Feast and Famine' Savings Model

Stop trying to force consistency. Embrace the lumpiness.

1. The Floor Contribution

Set a small, painful automatic transfer that happens every month no matter what.
Example: $200/month.
Why: It keeps the account active and maintains the psychological habit of saving, even in bad months.

2. The Skim (20%)

Every time you receive a commission or invoice payment:
- 30% to Tax Savings.
- 20% to Retirement (Solo 401k).
- 50% to Operating/Personal.
Result: A $20,000 month results in a $4,000 retirement contribution instantly.

3. The End-of-Year True-Up

In December, look at your total net profit. If you have excess cash in the business, make a lump-sum 'Employer Profit Sharing' contribution to max out your Solo 401(k) for the year. This lowers your tax bill immediately.

Tactical Adjustments

  1. Audit Your 'Good' Years: In a record year, do not upgrade your house. Act as if you earned your average income. Dump 100% of the surplus into VTI (Total Market Index). This buys you freedom for the bad years.
  2. Separate Accounts: Do not pay personal bills from business accounts. Transfer a flat 'Salary' to your personal checking. Save for retirement from the Business account (Solo 401k) or Personal account (Roth IRA) based on tax strategy.
  3. Tax-Loss Harvesting: Variable income pushes you into different tax brackets each year. In low-income years, do Roth Conversions. In high-income years, harvest losses in taxable accounts to offset income.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I retire early?

Yes, but your 'Freedom Number' should be higher (e.g., 30x expenses) to account for the lack of a steady pension or predictable catch-up phase.

What if I save $0 one year?

That happens. Don't beat yourself up. Just make sure you saved $40,000 the previous year when things were good. The average matters more than the frequency.

Is SEP IRA better?

It is simpler, but Solo 401(k) allows for 'Catch-Up' contributions ($7,500) if you are 50+, which SEP does not. Solo 401(k) is usually superior for aggressive savers.
